title: The wall broken down (Ephesians 2:11–22)
hookLine: Christ is our peace, breaking the dividing wall
tomorrow: kneel or stand to pray? the Bible has both. which is right?

cards: Some walls you can lean on. Others you can't see at all: who sits where, whose wedding you're invited to, which side of town you grew up on.
Paul writes that Christ "hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us." Here's the strange part. He never says which wall.
No street, no stones, no name. Just the middle wall, as if his readers would know. So which one was it?

teach.h: A TEMPLE BARRIER? THE LETTER DOESN'T SAY.
teach.b: Some readers think of a real one: a low stone barrier in the Jerusalem Temple, which the historian Josephus says warned foreigners not to go further. The letter itself never names it.
What Paul does name is the two peoples on either side.

He reminds Gentile believers they were once "far off," outside the promises God made to Israel, and now "are made nigh." Then: "For he is our peace, who hath made both one." Both: Jewish and Gentile believers.
Notice Paul doesn't call Christ a peacemaker who negotiates a truce. He says Christ is the peace. And the wall doesn't get a door cut in it, so one side can visit on certain days.
It comes down. Then the purpose: "for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace." Here's one to tell a friend: the Greek word behind man there is the everyday word for a human being.

teach.h: ONE NEW HUMANITY, OUT OF TWO.
teach.b: One new humanity, made out of two.
Then Paul trades walls for a house: "ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God." Not guests. Family.

Jewish readers understand God's covenant with Israel on their own terms, and this letter speaks of peace made in Christ. Which wall was it? Paul cares less about the stones than about what goes up in their place.

how: Some churches read Ephesians 2:14 at services for Christian unity or reconciliation, and some congregations of different backgrounds share worship or meals under its words, he is our peace.

games.q: what does “the wall broken down” mean?
o: a city wall knocked down by an army
a rule against fences between neighbors
Christ removing the barrier between two peoples

games.q: the wall and the house — tap the pairs.
p: one new humanity, out of two

s: Paul calls Christ a peacemaker who negotiates a truce
he says he is our peace: the peace itself, not a go-between.
the Greek behind 'one new man' is the everyday word for a human being
one new humanity, made out of two.
Paul calls Gentile believers fellowcitizens with the saints
no more strangers and foreigners, but of the household of God.

games.q: a friend says Paul's 'middle wall' was definitely a specific stone wall in the Temple. what's the fair answer?
o: some readers think so, but the letter itself never names one.
yes; Paul names the Temple wall in the very next verse.
no; Paul means the walls of Jericho from the book of Joshua.
games.why: some readers connect it to a Temple barrier that Josephus describes. the letter names only what the wall kept apart: two peoples, now made both one.

practice: Bring to mind one person a quiet wall has gone up with, built from a misunderstanding or just from time. Write them a short, plain text with no argument in it: thinking of you, or I miss our talks.
Hold it through the sit, and send it if it still feels right.

wordCard.voice: The wall broken down. Paul's picture of Christ removing the barrier between two peoples, and building one household.

orig.note: Greek: peace. Paul's word in he is our peace, Ephesians 2:14.

carryVoice: The line to keep: he is our peace, not a truce but a person. Take care.
